papers.title: A Dual Soft Attention Network for Automatic Sleep Staging via Single-Lead Electrocardiogram Signals.
papers.abstract: Polysomnography (PSG) is the current gold standard for sleep monitoring; however, it is complex, burdensome, and costly. In contrast, commercial health monitoring devices, such as the Apple Watch, offer sleep scoring at a low cost over a few days. This paper proposes a dual-attention mechanism-based sleep staging method using single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) signals, named SleepECGNet. The method extracts multi-scale features by employing convolutional kernels of different sizes, thereby capturing subtle details in the ECG signals. The model then integrates an SE module and a Luong attention-based encoder-decoder architecture to filter redundant information and dynamically focus on different sleep stages. Experiments were conducted using the HMC, MGH, and SHHS1 datasets for sleep staging tasks and the Apnea-ECG corpus was employed to execute transfer learning strategies directed at sleep apnea recognition. Comprehensive ablation experiments were conducted to verify the effectiveness of each component. Moreover, an analysis of sequence duration demonstrated that expanding the input timeframe directly improves classification outcomes.

papers.title: Machine learning and evolutionary computation for increased reliability of wearable devices for monitoring cardiac arrhythmias in the wild.
papers.journal: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine
papers.abstract: Continuous analysis of electrocardiogram (ECG) signals is essential for diagnosing cardiovascular diseases, particularly arrhythmias, which contribute significantly to global mortality. With the increasing use of wearable devices for non-clinical cardiac monitoring, real-time ECG processing encounters challenges due to memory constraints, particularly when memory is wasted by recording false positives. Noise in real-life ECG monitoring, such as motion artifacts, complicates automatic arrhythmia detection and recording, and calls for efficient methods to selectively filter out noisy signals that may be falsely classified (and recorded) as arrhythmias in devices with limited storage. This study develops and systematically compares machine learning and deep learning approaches for ECG noise detection using real-world wearable data acquired outside controlled clinical environments. By employing various models for classification, including Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, Multi-Layer Perceptron, Gradient Boosting and Convolutional Neural Networks, we investigated four approaches, using as input features: i) raw signal data, ii) Heart Rate Variability-related time-domain features, iii) a combination of Heart Rate Variability-related time-domain and frequency-domain features, and iv) the parameters of a Genetic Programming-based reconstruction algorithm, analyzing both memory and computational requirements and classification performance of the corresponding architectures. Our findings indicate that the Multilayer Perceptron model, combined with Heart Rate Variability-related time- and frequency-domain features, offers an optimal trade-off between accuracy, specificity, sensitivity, and F1-score. This study presents a scalable classification approach specifically designed for real-life arrhythmia detection in wearable devices, demonstrating the potential to enhance continuous cardiac monitoring and to facilitate the integration of such algorithms into wearable devices suitable for clinical and real-world settings.

papers.title: Language-supervised electrocardiogram interpretation with vision transformer.
papers.abstract:
PURPOSE: Most artificial intelligence models for electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation rely on task-specific supervised learning, requiring dedicated labeled datasets for each diagnostic task and limiting scalability across diverse cardiac conditions. This study investigated whether vision-language learning from paired ECG recordings and summary reports could enable transferable ECG representations without task-specific supervised training.

METHODS: We developed ECG-VLM, a contrastive vision-language model consisting of a Transformer-based image encoder and a text encoder, trained on 800,034 paired 10-s ECG recordings and summary reports from the MIMIC-IV-ECG database. Cardiac condition detection was performed using natural-language prompts without condition-specific retraining or fine-tuning. Performance was evaluated on an internal test set and externally validated using the LSAS-ECG dataset (45,151 recordings) across 14 cardiac conditions, together with retrieval and subgroup analysis.

RESULTS: ECG-VLM achieved diagnostic performance across 14 cardiac conditions, with AUROC ranging from 0.679 to 0.981 on the internal test set and from 0.691 to 0.991 on external validation. Performance was strongest for rhythm abnormalities (mean AUROC 0.948 internally and 0.921 externally) and lower for morphological conditions. Compared with the previously reported signal-based ECG-CLIP framework, ECG-VLM achieved comparable performance for rhythm abnormalities while improving AUPRC for several morphological conditions. Performance remained broadly consistent across external validation and demographic and clinical subgroups.

CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate the feasibility of vision-language supervision from paired ECG recordings and summary reports for learning transferable ECG representations without task-specific supervised training. This framework provides a basis for future extension of vision-language learning to ECG images encountered in routine clinical practice.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13755-026-00482-7.

papers.title: Memristor-based echo state network for ECG classification: optimizing accuracy and efficiency with different architectures.
papers.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) signal classification is a crucial task in automated cardiac monitoring and early disease detection. Conventional machine learning and deep learning methods often face challenges related to high computational costs, large data requirements and difficulty in handling real-time ECG analysis. In this work, we have proposed three memristor-based echo state network (MESN) models for ECG classification: (1) MESN, (2) Parallel MESNs (PMESN) with a classifier and (3) Attention-enhanced MESN (AMESN), where all three models employ artificial neural network (ANN) as a readout layer. These models leverage the property of an ESN to transform ECG signals into high-dimensional representations, thereby enhancing classification performance. The proposed models were evaluated on different benchmark ECG datasets: ECG200, ECG5000, ECGFiveDays, NonInvasiveFetalECGThorax1, NonInvasiveFetalECGThorax2, and TwoLeadECG. The results demonstrate that AMESN achieves the highest precision, recall, F1-score and overall accuracy particularly excelling in datasets with high intra-class variability. Whereas, PMESN improves robustness by leveraging multiple reservoir layers, while MESN provides a strong baseline with computational efficiency. These models are also compared with other state-of-the-art models and the analysis shows that AMESN achieves 1.92-13.39% higher accuracy, demonstrating superior performance. These findings highlight the potential of ESN as a lightweight yet powerful approach for ECG classification, making it suitable for integration into wearable and IoT-based healthcare systems.

papers.title: AI-based multimodal analysis of ECG and clinical data for evaluation for competitive sports participation: The VALETUDO trial.
papers.abstract:
AIMS: Pre-participation cardiovascular screening (PPS) is essential for preventing SCD in athletes, yet ECG interpretation requires expertise and remains resource-intensive. We aimed to evaluate the feasibility and diagnostic performance of a deep learning (DL) model for analysis of clinical data and resting 12‑lead ECG obtained during routine PPS in competitive athletes.

METHODS: In this prospective single center observational study, competitive athletes aged 18 to 60 years and undergoing routine PPS were enrolled. PPS included medical history, physical examination, resting and exercise ECG. Athletes were classified as fit or not fit for competitive sports according to clinical evaluation. Resting ECG and clinical variables were analyzed using a multimodal DL architecture. Model performance was assessed using stratified 10-fold cross-validation against PPS clinical classification.

RESULTS: A total of 526 athletes were enrolled (72% male, median age of 27 years (IQR: 20-41); 166 (32%) had a negative PPS result. The test setting (10-fold cross-validation), the model achieved moderate discrimination with an accuracy of 0.64 ± 0.08, SE 0.68 ± 0.15, SP 0.61 ± 0.17, F1-score 0.72 ± 0.1, PPV 0.80 ± 0.07, NPV 0.48 ± 0.12, AUC 0.72(0.66-0.78). Training performances reached accuracy of 0.70 ± 0.06, SE 0.73 ± 0.12, SP 0.67 ± 0.14, F1-score 0.77 ± 0.07, AUC 0.79 (0.74-0.83).

CONCLUSION: Automated DL-based analysis of 12‑lead ECG during PPS is feasible and showed encouraging diagnostic performance in competitive athletes. Although wider experience and external validation is required, AI-assisted multimodal ECG interpretation may represent a useful adjunct to physician assessment for cardiovascular risk stratification in sport screening programs.

papers.title: An adaptive multi-scale dilated convolutional neural network for arrhythmia detection.
papers.journal: Computer methods in biomechanics and biomedical engineering
papers.abstract: The rising global incidence of arrhythmia calls for reliable detection methods. Most existing approaches suffer from poor generalization and insufficient feature extraction for long-term electrocardiogram (ECG) signals. This work proposes an adaptive multi-scale dilated convolutional network (AMSDNet). It uses multi-scale dilated convolutions, gated adaptive weight allocation, and spatial attention fusion to capture global ECG features. Validated on Massachusetts Institute of Technology-Beth Israel Hospital Arrhythmia Database (MIT-BIH), the China Physiological Signal Challenge (CPSC) 2018, and the Computing in Cardiology Challenge (CINC) 2017 datasets, our method outperforms state-of-the-art models with average accuracy of 99.7%, 91.8% and 83.7%, respectively.

papers.title: Deep learning optimisation for cardiology: Neural Architecture Search-driven arrhythmia classification with electrocardiograms.
papers.abstract: Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death worldwide. Sudden cardiac death (SCD) accounts for roughly 50% of all cardiac deaths. The electrocardiogram (ECG) is widely used for diagnosing cardiac disease. However, the complexity of interpretation limits the ECG's efficacy. Modern deep learning methods can assist clinicians in diagnosis. We applied Neural Architecture Search (NAS) to identify optimal deep learning architectures for classifying cardiac arrhythmias with ECGs. We applied the Differentiable Architecture Search strategy to an AutoFormer search and trained, validated, and tested the resulting model on the PhysioNet Challenge 2021 (PC21) dataset (n = 88,253 from three continents). We optimised hyperparameters on the NAS output, exploring input patch size, class weighting, and loss function. The PC21 metric and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) are the performance metrics. The NAS converged towards minimal architectural configurations (embedding dimension: 384, depth: 4, self-attention heads: 4, MLP ratio: 1) with a validation and test PC21 metric of 0.66 (PC21 winner: 0.63). The NAS-created network achieved an AUROC of 0.97 and a PC21 metric of 0.72 during testing (PC21 winner: 0.69). We tested the PC21 winner architecture (1D-convolutional neural network with attention mechanism) without the attention mechanism and with the NAS-suggested architecture of 4 self-attention heads (instead of 8). The architecture without the attention mechanism performed similarly to the one with 8 self-attention heads (AUROC: 0.90, PC21 metric: 0.69). The architecture with 4 self-attention heads scored an AUROC of 0.91 and improved the PC21 metric to 0.71. The attention mechanism visualisation for two SCD-related arrhythmias (premature ventricular contractions and prolonged QT-interval) showed more clinically relevant attention for the 4-self-attention-head architectures. We interpret architectural simplicity as driving performance in arrhythmia classification. The self-attention mechanism can autonomously abstract clinical representations, simplifying clinical deployment by eliminating the need for an explicit feature-extraction pipeline.

papers.title: Deep learning and dual-domain fusion of temporal and spectrotemporal SCG for valvular heart disease classification.
papers.abstract: Heart valve disease (HVD) is a growing cause of cardiovascular morbidity, yet accessible screening tools remain limited. Tri-axial seismocardiogram (SCG) signals capture mechanical signatures of both stenosis and regurgitation, but their non-stationary nature and subtle inter-lesion morphological differences challenge robust classification from a single representation. This study proposes an electrocardiogram (ECG)-free dual-domain deep learning framework that combines a 1D convolutional-recurrent encoder of raw SCG waveforms with a 2D EfficientNet encoder of continuous wavelet transform scalograms, integrating temporal and spectrotemporal representations through feature-level fusion. The framework was evaluated on primary valve lesion classification in 94 patients, with an additional exploratory analysis of multi-valvular, aortic-stenosis-dominant disease. Under patient-level stratified group cross-validation, the fused model achieved the highest mean accuracy (65.3%; 95% CI, 59.8%-70.7%), exceeding both unimodal encoders and the majority-class (35.2%) and covariate-only (39.1%) baselines. The same mean performance ordering was preserved when the image backbone was replaced, although the confidence intervals overlap at this cohort size. Under the segment-level protocol used in prior studies, the framework achieved 99.63% accuracy, with faster training convergence and more compact, separable feature clusters than either unimodal encoder. These findings support the value of combining temporal and spectrotemporal SCG representations and demonstrate its potential for ECG-free HVD classification under patient-independent evaluation.

papers.title: Multiscale temporal deep learning for ECG waveform estimation from contactless radar signals.
papers.abstract: Electrocardiography (ECG) is widely used for monitoring cardiac activity and supporting the assessment of cardiovascularconditions. Conventional ECG systems require skin-contact electrodes, which may cause discomfort and limit their suitability forprolonged monitoring. Contactless radar sensing provides a non-contact approach for capturing chest-wall movements associatedwith cardiac activity. However, ECG waveform estimation from radar signals is challenging because radar measures mechanicalchest-wall motion, whereas ECG represents electrical cardiac activity. In addition, respiratory interference, motion artifacts, phasedistortion, and inter-subject variability can affect the relationship between radar and ECG signals. This study presents a multiscaletemporal deep learning framework for ECG waveform estimation from contactless radar signals. The proposed framework combinesradar signal preprocessing, feature extraction, multiscale residual convolutional learning, bidirectional long short-term memory(BiLSTM) networks, and multi-head attention to learn temporal and local signal representations from radar-derived features. Radarin-phase and quadrature (I/Q) signals are processed through phase extraction, denoising, and feature extraction to construct theinput representation for ECG estimation. The framework was evaluated using a publicly available synchronized radar-ECG datasetcontaining 30 subjects under the resting scenario. A subject-independent evaluation protocol was used, with separate participantsassigned to training, validation, and testing subsets. Across five repeated subject-independent randomized splits, the proposedframework achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.07584, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.14261 and Pearson correlationcoefficient (Pearson r) of 0.64459. These results demonstrate the feasibility of estimating the overall temporal structure of ECGwaveforms from contactless radar measurements under resting conditions.

papers.title: Deep Learning-Based BNP and NT-proBNP Evaluation From Wearable-Compatible Single-Lead ECGs for Heart Failure Assessment.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) and N-terminal pro-BNP (NT-proBNP) are critical biomarkers for diagnosing and managing heart failure. With the growing availability of wearable technologies, single-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) images have emerged as a practical and noninvasive source of clinical information. This study explores the use of a deep learning-based approach to estimate BNP and NT-proBNP levels from single-lead ECG images, aiming to support rapid, noninvasive screening in real-world settings.

METHODS: We analyzed 528,654 lead I ECGs from 237,686 unique patients within the Houston Methodist Health System, each paired with a corresponding BNP value obtained within 24 hours. A modified VGG16 convolutional neural network (CNN) was trained to classify BNP levels into clinically relevant thresholds: ≥100, ≥400, and ≥900 pg/mL. To prevent data leakage and ensure patient-level independence, the dataset was split by unique patients into training, validation, and testing sets. Additionally, the model's generalizability was evaluated by using an external Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC)-IV-ECG testing cohort comprising 18,549 unique patients and 42,377 electrocardiograms (ECGs) with corresponding NT-proBNP measurements, with predictions assessed against established NT-proBNP thresholds of ≥125, ≥450, and ≥900 pg/mL. We then examined the association between ECG-predicted BNP (ECG-BNP) and incident HF in 706,715 patients at Houston Methodist.

RESULTS: In the testing dataset, the model demonstrated robust performance, with area under the receiver operating characteristic (AUROC) values ranging from 0.84-0.86 and from 0.79-0.85 across the 3 classification thresholds of BNP and NT-proBNP, respectively. For the prediction of severe BNP elevation (≥900 pg/mL), the model achieved a sensitivity of 0.87 and a specificity of 0.70. The overall accuracy for distinguishing normal (<100 pg/mL) from elevated BNP levels (ie, ≥100 pg/mL) was 0.76. For NT-proBNP, the discriminative ability was higher at the lower cutoff (≥125 pg/mL) and declined slightly as thresholds increased, with AUROC values of 0.85, 0.82, and 0.79 for ≥125, ≥450, and ≥900 pg/mL, respectively. Consistent performance was observed across various demographic groups (sex and age categories) for all BNP and NT-proBNP thresholds. Higher baseline ECG-derived BNP levels were retrospectively associated with subsequent HF diagnosis across follow-up intervals extending up to 10 years, with stronger associations observed among patients whose baseline ECGs were temporally closer to HF diagnosis.

CONCLUSION: This study developed and validated a deep-learning model for classifying clinically relevant BNP and NT-proBNP thresholds from single-lead ECG images. The model demonstrated strong discrimination and external validation, supporting further investigation of single-lead ECG-derived natriuretic peptide classification for scalable cardiovascular screening and risk assessment.

papers.title: Patient-adaptive and clinically interpretable arrhythmia detection from ECG using lightweight hybrid deep learning.
papers.abstract: A precise and reliable identification of cardiac arrhythmias from electrocardiogram (ECG) signals is critical for making informed clinical decisions. In this paper, a patient-adaptive and clinically interpretable a hybrid CNN-LSTM model with an attention mechanism is offered as a framework for ECG arrhythmia identification. The proposed framework combines signal preprocessing techniques with domain knowledge-driven morphological and time-frequency features to jointly analyze the waveform patterns and temporal dependencies in noisy ECG signals. In addition to beat-level classification, a composite arrhythmia burden score is also proposed to offer a patient-level summary of arrhythmic activity, and a lightweight patient-specific adaptation method is used to enhance reliability with limited calibration data. Over 99% accuracy and strong sensitivity to ventricular and supraventricular arrhythmias are demonstrated by experimental results employing a rigorous inter-patient methodology on the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database. The suggested framework's capacity to generalize on actual clinical datasets is further validated by external validation on the PTB-XL dataset without retraining. The proposed framework is also scalable for cloud-based deployment to enable continuous ECG monitoring, thus emphasizing its potential for practical and patient-centric cardiac care.

papers.title: JEPA-Mamba: a self-supervised joint-embedding architecture with bidirectional Mamba for ECG representation learning.
papers.abstract:
UNLABELLED: The electrocardiogram (ECG) is the primary non-invasive tool for early screening and clinical management of cardiovascular disease, but deep learning deployment is limited by scarce labeled data, by architectures that ignore the periodic structure of ECG signals, and by the trade-off between long-sequence efficiency and diagnostic accuracy. We propose JEPA-Mamba, a self-supervised representation learning framework that integrates the Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) with a bidirectional Mamba encoder and a channel-temporal attention module (CTAM) for multi-adaptive ECG classification on downstream tasks. High-ratio contiguous-block masking trains an exponential moving average (EMA) encoder and a narrow predictor to learn diagnostic features without hand-crafted augmentation, while the bidirectional Mamba (BiM) encoder, augmented by rotary position embedding (RoPE) and a register mechanism, couples convolutional waveform extraction with linear-complexity long-sequence modeling and CTAM recalibrates the 12 leads and focuses temporal attention on clinically salient segments. Under a strict patient-level split on PTB-XL, with an encoder pretrained on MIMIC-IV-ECG for cross-dataset validation on the same tasks, JEPA-Mamba attains macro-averaged AUCs of 0.9296 ± 0.002 and 0.9306 ± 0.002 on the fully annotated task, outperforming self-supervised baselines on most downstream tasks and surpassing the most direct JEPA counterpart in the ECG domain across all tasks. Improvements over external baselines on the all, Sub-diag., and Diag. tasks are statistically significant, and internal ablation differences are confirmed by DeLong tests. Per-class analyses, attention maps, t-SNE embeddings, and robustness experiments under noise and baseline drift support these design choices. These results offer preliminary evidence for the clinical potential of JEPA-Mamba.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s13534-026-00620-w.

papers.title: Deep learning analysis of sinus-rhythm echocardiography for the identification of patients with atrial fibrillation.
papers.abstract:
AIMS: Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (AF) is underdiagnosed due to its intermittent and asymptomatic nature. We evaluated whether a deep neural network (DNN) applied to transthoracic echocardiograms (TTEs) acquired in sinus rhythm can discriminate between patients with and without documented AF and identify individuals at increased risk for subsequent AF documentation and adverse outcomes.

METHODS AND RESULTS: We retrospectively analysed 85 686 TTE studies (2009-21). A DNN was applied to apical four-chamber and parasternal long-axis videos without Doppler. AF ground truth was based on International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes, electrocardiogram, Holter, or prior echocardiographic documentation of AF. The dataset was split into training (60%), validation (20%), and an independent test set (20%). In the test cohort, we assessed discrimination performance. Among patients without prior AF, we evaluated associations between model classification and subsequent AF documentation and a composite outcome of all-cause mortality, heart failure hospitalization, or stroke. The test set included 17 121 patients (median age 66 years [interquartile range, IQR 54-75]; 57.6% male), of whom 3449 (20.1%) had prior AF. The model achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.85, with sensitivity 0.80 and specificity 0.72. At the selected threshold, 6581 patients (38.4%) were classified as model-positive, including 3832 (58.2%) without prior AF. Among patients without prior AF, model-positive classification was associated with subsequent AF documentation [adjusted hazard ratio (HR) 1.64; 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.33-2.04] and with the composite outcome (adjusted HR 1.24; 95% CI 1.13-1.35).

CONCLUSION: Deep learning applied to sinus-rhythm TTE demonstrates discrimination for AF and identifies an imaging-derived signal associated with subsequent AF documentation and adverse outcomes.

papers.title: ReBAN-Net: An interpretable hybrid deep learning framework for ECG-based emotion recognition.
papers.abstract: Emotional assessment is essential for mental health management, yet questionnaire-based scales are subjective and facial- or voice-based approaches can be influenced by intentional behavior and environmental interference. This study proposes ReBAN-Net, a hybrid architecture integrating a one-dimensional residual convolutional network, a bidirectional long short-term memory network, and a soft attention mechanism for ECG-based emotion recognition. Three classification tasks were defined throughout the study: nine-class valence classification (levels 1-9), nine-class arousal classification (levels 1-9), and four-class affective-state classification (baseline, stress, amusement, and meditation). The model was evaluated on the WESAD dataset using a strict 15-fold leave-one-subject-out protocol. It achieved accuracies of 86.03% for nine-class valence, 86.27% for nine-class arousal, and 87.58% for four-class affective-state classification, with corresponding macro-AUC values of 96.07%, 96.24%, and 95.09%. Temporal class activation and attention-feature analyses show that the model focuses on physiologically meaningful ECG regions. These results demonstrate the feasibility and interpretability of ReBAN-Net and indicate its potential for subject-independent ECG-based emotion recognition.

papers.title: A clinical decision support system for ECG diagnosis: Surpassing commercial standards through dual-stream feature fusion.
papers.journal: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Automated electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation is essential for clinical efficiency, yet many existing deep learning (DL) models are perceived as "black boxes" and lack direct benchmarking against established commercial standards. To foster clinician trust and support reimbursement justification, AI systems must demonstrate not only superior accuracy but also alignment with established clinical criteria.

METHODS: We proposed a Dual-Stream Signal Fusion Architecture that integrates latent spatio-temporal features from 21,799 raw 12-lead ECG waveforms (PTB-XL) with 148 expert-engineered clinical metrics extracted via commercial algorithms (PTB-XL+). The system was evaluated against the Marquette 12SL™ (12SL) commercial standard using the independent PTB-XL test set (Fold 10).

RESULTS: The proposed Hybrid Model achieved a Macro F1-Score of 0.851, significantly outperforming the commercial 12SL standard (0.812) and the waveform-only baseline (0.821). Notably, sensitivity for Myocardial Infarction (MI) improved by 10.8% relative to 12SL (0.72 vs. 0.65). Feature importance analysis confirmed that the model's decisions are clinically traceable, attributing 45% importance to QRS amplitude for Hypertrophy diagnosis, which aligns with Sokolow-Lyon criteria.

CONCLUSIONS: Our hybrid framework offers a superior, transparent, and robust standard for automated ECG interpretation. By outperforming clinical gold standards and providing physiologically sound reasoning, this work represents a step toward building the clinical evidence base for AI-based diagnostic support across diverse global populations; prospective, multi-site validation remains necessary before clinical deployment can be considered. The proposed framework is further distinguished by its modular design, which ensures adaptability across both resource-rich and resource-limited clinical environments.
